questions.prompt: What is the strongest argument for readable code?
choices: You will be the one reading it when it breaks, months from now
questions.explain: Code is read far more often than it is written, and usually by someone who has forgotten why it was written that way. That someone is normally you.

questions.prompt: Which of these make a function easier to test?
choices: It returns a value rather than printing one
It reads its inputs from parameters rather than from globals
It is as short as possible regardless of what it does
questions.explain: The first three each remove something a test would otherwise have to work around. Shortness for its own sake tends to split one clear function into two unclear ones.

questions.prompt: When is a comment worth writing?
choices: When it explains why the code does something, not what it does
Only at the top of the file
questions.explain: The what is already in the code and cannot go stale. The why -- the constraint, the bug this works around, the decision that was not obvious -- exists nowhere else.

questions.prompt: Changing the shape of code without changing what it does is called ___.
questions.explain: Keeping behaviour fixed is what makes it safe. It is also why refactoring is the last step of the test-driven cycle rather than the first: the tests are what prove the behaviour did not move.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson pair code quality with testing rather than treating them separately?
choices: Tests are what let you improve code without fear of breaking it
questions.explain: Without tests, every tidy-up is a risk, so the code ossifies. The suite is what turns a change you are nervous about into one you can make and verify.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Running the suite often is what makes a break traceable to the change that caused it. Say what that is worth.

reflection-exercise2.hint: A test nobody trusts is worse than no test, because it is still costing time. Say what you do when one goes stale.
